work.title: The Life of Timon of Athens
work.author: William Shakespeare

scene.label: Act 5, Scene 1
scene.title: SCENE I. The woods. Before Timon's cave

lines.text: As I took note of the place, it cannot be far where he abides.
lines.plainText: As I took note of the place it cannot be far where he abides

lines.text: What's to be thought of him? Does the rumour hold for true that he is so full of gold?
lines.plainText: What's to be thought of him Does the rumour hold for true that he is so full of gold

lines.text: Certain. Alcibiades reports it; Phrynia and Timandra had gold of him. He likewise enriched poor straggling soldiers with great quantity. 'Tis said he gave unto his steward a mighty sum.
lines.plainText: Certain Alcibiades reports it Phrynia and Timandra had gold of him He likewise enriched poor straggling soldiers with great quantity 'Tis said he gave unto his steward a mighty sum

lines.text: Then this breaking of his has been but a try for his friends?

lines.text: Nothing else. You shall see him a palm in Athens again, and flourish with the highest. Therefore 'tis not amiss we tender our loves to him in this supposed distress of his. It will show honestly in us and is very likely to load our purposes with what they travail for, if it be a just and true report that goes of his having.

lines.text: What have you now to present unto him?

lines.text: Nothing at this time but my visitation; only I will promise him an excellent piece.

lines.text: Good as the best. Promising is the very air o' th' time; it opens the eyes of expectation. Performance is ever the duller for his act and, but in the plainer and simpler kind of people, the deed of saying is quite out of use. To promise is most courtly and fashionable; performance is a kind of will or testament which argues a great sickness in his judgment that makes it.

lines.text: I am thinking what I shall say I have provided for him. It must be a personating of himself, a satire against the softness of prosperity, with a discovery of the infinite flatteries that follow youth and opulency.

lines.text: [Aside.] Must thou needs stand for a villain in thine own work? Wilt thou whip thine own faults in other men? Do so, I have gold for thee.
